name: Sejong the Great
info: Sejong (1397–1450), known as Sejong the Great, was the fourth king of Joseon, reigning from 1418 to 1450, remembered above all for the creation of Hangul and for a reign of advances in science, medicine and agriculture.

facts.born: 15 May 1397 (the 10th day, 4th month) in Chunsubang, Hanyang (Seoul); born Yi To, third son of Grand Prince Chŏngan, the future King Taejong, and Princess Chŏngnyŏng
facts.died: 8 April 1450 (the 17th day, 2nd month), aged 52, after long illness, in the residence of Grand Prince Yŏngŭng in Gyeongbokgung; buried at Yeongneung
facts.role: Prince Ch'ungnyŏng (1408), Grand Prince (1413), crown prince (1418); fourth king of Joseon, 1418–1450
facts.known: The creation of Hangul and the Hunminjeongeum (1446); the Hall of Worthies; the rain gauge, water clock and Ch'ilchŏngsan calendar; the medical texts Hyangyakchipsŏngbang and Ŭibangyuch'wi; the kongpŏp tax reform; the Ōei Invasion of Tsushima and the northern frontier

t: Sejong, the fourth king of Joseon, reigned from 1418 to 1450 and is widely regarded as the greatest king in Korean history.

He is remembered above all for Hangul, the Korean alphabet published in 1446, and for a reign in which his court produced a native calendar, a rain gauge, vast medical and agricultural texts and new movable type.
He governed by Confucian principles and restricted Buddhist institutions while privately practising Buddhism, and North Korean histories stress the feudal burdens on the peasantry under his rule.
dyk: In 1430 Sejong had over 170,000 people polled on a proposed tax reform; the debate that followed lasted 17 years.
ev: Sejong's elder brother Yangnyŏng is deposed; Sejong becomes crown prince and then king when Taejong abdicates
Sejong launches the Ōei Invasion against Tsushima Island
Sejong re-establishes the Hall of Worthies
A campaign under Kim Chongsŏ against the Jurchens leads to six garrisons on the northern frontier
The rain gauge ch'ŭgugi is invented at court
The kongpŏp tax system is completed, lowering the land tax from 10% of the harvest to 5%
Hangul is published in the Hunminjeongeum and its commentary, the Hunminjeongeum Haerye
Sejong dies, the first Joseon king to die in office, and is succeeded by Munjong

sections.early:
Sejong was born Yi To on the 10th day of the 4th month of 1397 in Chunsubang, Hanyang (Seoul), five years after the founding of Joseon. He was the third son of Grand Prince Chŏngan, the fifth son of the founding king Taejo, and of Princess Chŏngnyŏng. His father had played a major role in founding the dynasty, launched the First Strife of the Princes in 1398 and took the throne in 1400 as King Taejong.

Very little is known of his early life, as it long seemed unlikely that he would rule. One anecdote, which several historians judge possibly fanciful and Gari Ledyard plausible, tells that he read so much that his father took away his books, and that he read the one book left behind several times over. In 1408 he was made Prince Ch'ungnyŏng, and in 1413 Grand Prince. By then he was considered bright and skilled at calligraphy, the gayageum and painting, and he began to be tutored by the scholar-official Yi Su. Taejong told him that year that he had "nothing to do in particular" and should enjoy his life in peace. In early 1418 his younger brother, Grand Prince Sŏngnyŏng, fell deathly ill, and Ch'ungnyŏng reportedly stayed by his bed day and night, reading medical texts and helping with the treatment.
sections.rise:
Taejong had designated his eldest son, Grand Prince Yangnyŏng, as heir, but anecdotes record that Yangnyŏng disobeyed the king, neglected his studies and womanized, while the Veritable Records of Taejong show Ch'ungnyŏng praised as intelligent and studious. The brothers developed a bitter rivalry. In 1417 Yangnyŏng's affair with Ŏri, a concubine of the official Kwak Sŏn, enraged Taejong, and in 1418 Yangnyŏng brought her back into the palace, where she bore his child. After a letter in which Yangnyŏng questioned his father's judgement, Taejong and his ministers met on the 3rd day of the 6th month of 1418 and, overriding primogeniture, demoted and exiled him.

Taejong then nominated Ch'ungnyŏng as the more able of his sons, and the court reportedly agreed with enthusiasm. On the 10th day of the 8th month of 1418 Taejong abdicated, and the 21-year-old prince took the throne at Gyeongbokgung. As king emeritus, Taejong kept a veto over all decisions and tight control of the military until his death in 1422. Several historians argue that Sejong's reign rested on the stability his father's statecraft had created.
sections.deeds:
In 1420 Sejong re-established the Hall of Worthies, likened by modern historians to a think tank, which oversaw the court's great projects. Under his reign an armillary sphere (1433), a water clock designed by Chang Yŏngsil (1434), the rain gauge ch'ŭgugi (1441) and a stream gauge were made, and in 1444 the court devised Korea's first native calendar, Ch'ilchŏngsan, with Seoul as its reference point. The 56-volume Hyangyakchipsŏngbang (1433) described over 10,000 treatments, and the 365-volume Ŭibangyuch'wi followed. In 1434 more than 200,000 copper kabin types were cast, and the 1429 Nongsa chiksŏl adapted farming knowledge to Korea.

His tax reform, kongpŏp, was designed from 1427, put to a survey of over 170,000 people in 1430 and completed in 1444, lowering the land tax from 10% of the harvest to 5%. He granted government serf women 100 days of maternity leave in 1426, later adding paternity leave for their husbands, and set rules for clean prisons. Abroad, the 1419 Ōei Invasion against Tsushima, with 227 ships and some 17,000 soldiers, was followed by decades of peace and trade with Japan, and campaigns against the Jurchens in 1433 and 1437 brought the northern border to roughly its present line. In the 12th month of 1443 he revealed Hangul to his court.
sections.opponents:
Sejong's chief critics were Confucian officials of his own court. In 1444 a faction of the Hall of Worthies led by Ch'oe Malli rebuked Hangul as anti-Confucian and too far a departure from Chinese civilization; anti-Hangul sentiment was also partly elitist, as literacy in Hanja marked status. Sejong had Ch'oe and several others imprisoned for a single day. His private Buddhism set him against officials who, like Yun Hoe in 1424, called Buddhism the worst of heterodox teachings; in 1439 a petition signed by 648 Confucian students and scholars protested his repair of the temple Heungcheonsa, and he assured them he "had never worshipped the Buddha".

Yet his own policies weighed heavily on others. He cut the Buddhist schools from seven to two in 1424, closed all but 18 temples of each, melted down bells and statues for weapons and barred monks from the capital, a ban that lasted until the late 19th century. In 1427 he forced the Huihui, Korea's Muslim community, to abandon their headgear and close their mosque in Kaesong. His attempts to raise the marginalized ch'ŏnmin failed, and his northern settlements had mixed success, as Korean settlers often abandoned the land. North Korean histories hold that his rule brought heightened feudal subjugation and heavier taxes for the peasantry.
sections.last:
Sejong suffered recurring and worsening ill health for much of his life: back and knee pain from his early twenties, then problems with his vision, excess thirst and excess urination. Most scholars suppose he had diabetes, though the medical researcher JiHwan Lee argues his symptoms better fit ankylosing spondylitis. From 1437 he asked to delegate lesser affairs to the crown prince, and in 1439 he stopped attending the royal lectures. His ministers resisted, and after an edict of 1443 met furious protest, the crown prince began to handle routine government only in 1445. Historian Kim Jongmyung argues that Sejong then devoted himself to Hangul.

The deaths of his sons Grand Prince Kwangp'yŏng in 1444 and Grand Prince P'yŏngwŏn in 1445, and of Queen Sohŏn in 1446, deepened his Buddhism; he practised Buddhist vegetarianism, built a shrine on the palace grounds and in 1449 invited the monk Sinmi to hold services. He died on the 17th day of the 2nd month of 1450, aged 52, the first Joseon king to die in office. He was buried at Yeongneung beside Queen Sohŏn, and his son Munjong succeeded him.
sections.legacy:
Sejong has been judged by a number of historians the greatest monarch in Korean history, and his reign is often called a golden age; his name appears in the Veritable Records over 2,000 times, more than any other Joseon king's. Hangul, however, was long looked down upon and was officially adopted by the government only in 1894, during the Kabo Reform. His practice of making extra copies of the Veritable Records saved them for later historians, since most copies were destroyed by the Japanese in 1592.

In South Korea he is an icon of national culture: Hangul Day, every 9 October, celebrates his alphabet; Sejong City, Sejong Street and King Sejong Station in Antarctica bear his name; a 9.5-metre bronze statue stands in Gwanghwamun Square; and his portrait has been on the 10,000-won note since 1973. James Palais argued that he was no despot but bested his critics "at their own game". North Korean writings discuss him less and more negatively: one history praises Hangul's linguistic features but credits its development to the intellect of the masses, and another says that everything he did served to consolidate feudalism.

summary: Sejong ruled Joseon from 1418 to 1450, overseeing advances in astronomy, medicine, printing, agriculture and law, a lighter land tax, peace with Japan and an expanded northern frontier. He created Hangul, published in 1446, against opposition at his court, and is widely regarded as Korea's greatest king.

notes: The article gives birth and death both as Gregorian (May 15, 1397 – April 8, 1450, in the lead) and as lunar dates (10th day 4th month 1397; 17th day 2nd month 1450). Both kept in the facts.
Dates of the Ŭibangyuch'wi (1445 or 1447) and the Ganuidae observatory (1434 or 1438) are disputed in the article; I gave no year for the first and left out the second.
The 'greatest king' judgement is attributed to historians as the article does.
